note: The adversarial findings register of the PR #17 audit. verification says how far a finding is established: REPRODUCED (shown failing by a test or a script), CONFIRMED (established by reading the code, not executed), POTENTIAL (suspected, not established), BLOCKED (cannot be established here, and why), NOT_REPRODUCED (looked for and not found). resolution says what became of it: OPEN, FIXED (with the commit and regression test), DOCUMENTED (a limit stated, not a defect to fix here), OWNER (needs an owner decision or action), NOT_A_DEFECT.

severity_scale.P0: authority bypass, integrity failure, credential exposure, security-boundary violation, silent data corruption or unauthorized external effect
severity_scale.P1: incorrect recovery, replay disagreement, unsafe concurrency, false verification claim, scientific correctness defect, or unbounded scaling on a required operation
severity_scale.P2: test gap, performance, maintainability, or a documentary inconsistency with practical consequences
severity_scale.P3: optional future enhancement, or information an owner should have

findings.title: Six commit histories exist only inside deleted bundle files
findings.behavior: The PR deletes twelve git bundle files from the tree. The heads e0e71ce, c3b59bb, cf813b0, 7d85223, d2a71b0 and a0566d7 are not commits of this repository on any of its 13 remote branches; they exist only inside those bundle blobs.
findings.invariant: Removing a retired artefact from the active tree must not destroy the only copy of history the owner may need.
findings.mechanism: Deleting the files from the PR head destroys nothing: main's tree and history still hold the blobs. The PR description lists purging the retired programme from history as an owner choice. A purge that removed these blobs would remove the only copies of those six histories.
findings.reproduction: git bundle list-heads on each blob; git cat-file -e <head>^{commit} in a full clone with every remote branch fetched.
findings.observed: 6 bundle heads absent from the repository's own history.
findings.expected: Either the histories are archived outside the repository before any purge, or they are declared expendable.
findings.correction: None in this PR. An owner who purges history should first archive the bundles, or the six histories, elsewhere.
findings.residual_risk: Loss of retired-programme history on an owner-run purge.

findings.title: A final record that lost only its trailing newline verifies, and the next append fuses two records into one unparseable line
findings.behavior: read() splits the file into lines and accepts a final line that parses even when it has no trailing newline. _write_event opens the log in append mode and writes the next record without checking that the file ends with a newline. Its own short-write branch raises and leaves the written bytes on disk, which can be every byte but the newline.
findings.invariant: A record is durable on return and stays readable; a crash or short write leaves at most a torn tail that refuses appends until repaired (D-2026-50).
findings.mechanism: The state 'complete record, newline missing' reads as a clean log (ok=True, every record counted). The next append returns normally and its bytes are glued to the unterminated line, so the last two records become one unparseable final line.
findings.reproduction: An EventLog with three appends; truncate the file's final byte; verify(); append once more; verify() again. Script recorded in the audit's session notes (scratchpad repro/torn_newline.py); regression test added with the fix.
findings.observed: After the lost newline: ok=True, count=3. After the next append (which returned): ok=False, count=2, a 'partial final record' and 'TRUNCATED: witness records seq 3 but the log ends at 1'. Seq 2 and the acknowledged seq 3 are unreadable, and the log refuses every later append.
findings.expected: An unterminated final line is a torn tail: the read refuses it as such (the records before it intact), appends refuse until the tail is repaired, and no append ever lands after unterminated bytes.
findings.correction: One line rule for every reader (_parse_line in agent_substrate/events.py): a record ends in its newline, so an unterminated final line is a torn tail in the whole-chain read (TruncatedTail, the records before it intact) and refused by the anchored tail read; and the write path refuses to write when the byte before end-of-file is not a newline, under the writer lock, after the head check.
findings.residual_risk: The write-side guard closes the window between the head check and the write for writers of this class; flock stays advisory, so a process that writes the file without the lock can still interleave bytes mid-write, as the module docstring states.

findings.title: anchor_at() builds an anchor from a second, unverified read, and nothing binds it to the read that was verified
findings.behavior: anchor_at(seq) re-reads the log, finds the record at seq and checks only that it hashes to its own stored hash: no link before it, no witness. Its docstring says an anchor is worth trusting 'because something verified the log to produce it'. Twelve call sites take a verified read, fold it, and then call anchor_at for the position they reached, and checkpoint.create() verifies the log and then anchors from a separate read; none compares the anchor's hash with the hash of the event it folded or verified.
findings.invariant: An anchor (and a checkpoint marked full_verification) describes bytes a verification actually covered.
findings.mechanism: A rewrite of the file between the verified read and anchor_at produces an anchor at a record the verification never saw; every later advance() and verify_from() trusts the prefix before it. Honest concurrent writers only append, so this needs a writer that rewrites the file during the window. Anchored reads already trust the prefix, so this widens a trust the design states rather than creating a new one.
findings.reproduction: By reading: no comparison of anchor.head_hash with the verified event's hash at any of the 12 call sites or in checkpoint.create().
findings.observed: Anchors and checkpoints carry the hash of a record re-read after verification.
findings.expected: The anchor is taken from the verified read itself, or anchor_at is told the hash it must find.
findings.correction: VerifyReport.verified_anchor: the verified read returns an anchor at the last record it verified, from the bytes it parsed. The 13 projection sites and checkpoint.create() take it instead of a second read; anchor_at(seq, head_hash=...) refuses a record other than the one named, and checkpoint.create(require_full_verification=False) binds its anchor to the witness's hash.
findings.residual_risk: anchor_at() without head_hash is still the unbound slow path, used by tests; no production module calls it without head_hash.

findings.title: Invariant I3 says re-verification after STALE needs fresh evidence; the evidence merge lets the pre-staleness report satisfy it
findings.behavior: Both the live transition and the replay evaluate an edge against {**record.evidence, **transition.evidence}. After STALE, UNDER_REVIEW -> VERIFIED requires 'verification_report', which the record already carries from before it went stale.
findings.invariant: I3: STALE returns to PROMOTED only through VERIFIED, 'which requires fresh evidence' -- the prior verification no longer describes the current inputs.
findings.mechanism: A record verified with report R, promoted, made STALE by a dependency change, re-reviewed, and re-verified with an empty evidence mapping is VERIFIED again on R, and can be promoted again on R. The second reader restates the same rule and agrees, so nothing flags it.
findings.reproduction: scratchpad repro/fresh_evidence.py against f142a7e and the fix; repro/stale_reverify.py.
findings.observed: Before (f142a7e): re-verification after STALE with evidence={} -> VERIFIED; citing the same report again -> VERIFIED; a history with that transition appended past the gate loads in the store, and the second reader holds the record VERIFIED with nothing unauthorized. A first verification resting on a report the proposer attached at creation was likewise accepted.
findings.expected: UNDER_REVIEW -> VERIFIED cites a verification_report the transition itself supplies and the record did not already carry; refused live and on replay, by both readers.
findings.correction: Edge.requires_fresh on UNDER_REVIEW -> VERIFIED ({'verification_report'}), judged by check() against TransitionRequest.prior_evidence -- the record's evidence before the transition -- which both store call sites pass. The second reader restates it (_Rule.fresh, _auth_refusal(prior=...)). For scientific results the admission rule already refused re-admission when the result's own governed run had been invalidated; a result made STALE by a dependency had no such cover, and the edge rule covers every kind. Fresh means other bytes. An independent check is deterministic: run again on the same bundle by the same checker it produced a byte-identical report under a new governed task (tests/test_scientific_invalidation.py), and the report names the verifier's implementation, the subject and the result. Identical bytes are the same verification, which cannot describe what made the record stale, so it is refused; a changed checker or changed inputs produce other bytes and are fresh.
regression_tests: tests/test_scientific_invalidation.py::test_a_stale_result_is_not_reused_and_not_readmitted (the stale report and a byte-identical re-check refused by I3; the origin rule shown on a record citing the withdrawn run)
findings.residual_risk: Freshness is judged against the report the record carries now, so a report used for an earlier verification and later replaced could be cited again after a second staleness. TransitionRequest.prior_evidence defaults to empty for direct callers (tests, tools/model_check.py), the first verification's case; every production construction passes it, held by a structural test. No committed history exists to migrate; a history written before this rule that re-verified on an inherited report no longer replays. Three fixtures verified a record on a report it was created with, or re-cited the stale one; they now follow the honest workflow: tests/test_agent_crash_recovery.py, tests/test_governed_model_reuse.py, tests/test_scientific_invalidation.py.

findings.title: The log accepted any encoding of a record, and its readers did not agree where records begin
findings.behavior: Every reader recomputes the hash over the PARSED record, so any byte string that parses to it verified: other whitespace, key order or escapes, and a key given twice (json keeps the last value, which the hash covers; a first-wins parser shows the first). read() split lines with bytes.splitlines(), which also breaks at a CR; anchor_at, _read_anchored and _read_tail iterate the file, which breaks only at a newline.
findings.invariant: canonical.py: every integrity claim reduces to 'are these the same bytes'. _validate_field_types already refuses an unhashed extra field because it 'could carry unverified content beside a valid digest'; a duplicated key is the same thing.
findings.mechanism: The hash binds the parse, not the line; and the two framings disagree on bytes containing a CR.
findings.reproduction: scratchpad repro/event_log_framing.py, run against c11c628 and against the fix (before/after table in docs/audit/AUDIT_PROGRESS.md).
findings.observed: Before: a CR in place of a newline verified in full (count 3) while anchor_at(1) raised a bare JSONDecodeError; a CR in a record's whitespace verified from an anchor and failed in full; a duplicated actor key verified, the fold saw 'a' and a first-wins parser 'mallory'; a record re-encoded with spaces and reversed keys verified.
findings.expected: A record is its canonical bytes and one newline, framed at the newline only, the same in every reader.
findings.correction: _parse_line: the one statement of what a line is, used by all five readers; it refuses a line that is not exactly canonical_bytes(record) + b'\n'. The whole-chain reader frames at b'\n' only.
findings.residual_risk: Blank lines between records are still skipped, as before; they carry no content. No committed event log exists in the repository to migrate (checked: 0 files with event records).

findings.title: A live projection folds a rewritten history onto the state it built from the old one, and can then write a record that makes the log unreplayable
findings.behavior: Catching up, a projection folds only records whose seq is above its position and assumes every record at or below it is one it already folded. On an anchor mismatch it falls back to a full verified read and keeps that assumption. When its anchor lags its position -- the records it appended itself -- advance() succeeds without any mismatch at all.
findings.invariant: A projection is disposable: what a live projection holds, and decides against, is what a fresh replay of the same log yields.
findings.mechanism: Nothing compares the history being caught up from with the history already folded. A restore of the log and its witness from a backup -- an operational act, not an attack -- replaces the records below the position with others.
findings.reproduction: scratchpad repro/rewritten_prefix.py: create r0; back up log and witness; create r1; a second process loads; restore the backup; an honest writer creates r2 and r3; the second process catches up and transitions r1.
findings.observed: Live projection after catching up: r0, r1, r3; a fresh replay of the same log: r0, r2, r3. The live projection then appended a transition on r1, which the log never created, and every fresh load of that log fails with KeyError 'r1'.
findings.expected: Catching up refuses -- the projection stays refused until load() -- when the log no longer extends the history the projection folded.
findings.correction: events.require_extends(): before a catch-up folds anything, the log must still hold the record at the projection's position with the hash the projection folded there -- equivalently, since the chain is verified, everything below it. Each projection keeps that hash beside its position (AuthorityStore._loaded_hash, Scheduler._seen_hash, _folded_hash in the agent directory, policy store, memory store, proposal ingress, idempotency ledger and every DecidedWriter), set wherever the position moves, including a projection's own appends. Both catch-up routes call it. The refusal is remembered by projection_fold until load().
findings.residual_risk: The proposal ingress and the idempotency ledger rebuild from scratch on the full-read route, as they did before; they now refuse on the anchored route. A restore is refused by a live process, not reported anywhere else: a process started after the restore reads the restored history as the history, which is the no-external-trust-root limit the witness work (Phase 3) addresses. GovernedTasks keeps its own catch-up (_after_move), whose anchor is the record it folded last and whose fallback is a full replay; it was not changed.
mutations: tools/mutations/agent_incremental.json: N12-N27 (the check's two refusals and each of the 14 call sites)
tools/mutations/agent_snapshot_coherence.json: V_store_fallback, V_scheduler_fallback (anchors moved past the new check)

findings.title: Replaying a record the reducer cannot read raises a bare KeyError or ValueError in the primary store, and the second reader applies one of them
findings.behavior: Seven malformed authority records -- a transition of a record never created; a create or transition without record_id; a transition without dst, with a dst that is no state, or without role; a dependency without depends_on -- each made AuthorityStore.load() raise a bare KeyError or ValueError. The second reader reported six as anomalies and applied the seventh, a dependency naming no dependency, as an empty one.
findings.invariant: Every refusal of a history by the store is a StoreError, so a caller that catches StoreError catches every refusal.
findings.mechanism: A missing membership check in one of two parallel branches.
findings.observed: Primary: KeyError('ghost'), KeyError('record_id') twice, KeyError('dst'), ValueError('NOT_A_STATE' is not a valid State), KeyError('role'), KeyError('depends_on'). Second reader: anomalies for six, none for the dependency without depends_on.
findings.expected: Both readers refuse each: the store with a StoreError naming the seq, the second reader with an anomaly.
findings.correction: AuthorityStore._apply turns a KeyError, TypeError or ValueError raised while folding into a StoreError naming the seq and action, and the transition branch refuses a record never created by name, as the dependency branch did. reconstruct.py reports a dependency record without depends_on as an anomaly and does not apply it.
findings.residual_risk: The wrapper converts the error's type, not its cause: a KeyError from a defect in the reducer itself is now reported as an unreadable record, with the original chained.

findings.title: The event append() returns is not the event a replay reads: the caller's tuples and int keys come back from the log as lists and strings, under the same hash
findings.behavior: _write_event hashed the caller's body and returned an Event holding the caller's Python values. canonical_bytes serializes an int, float, bool or None dict key as a string and a tuple as a list, so the record a replay parses is a different Python value with the same hash. Every projection folds its own append from the returned Event.
findings.invariant: canonical.py: two records that differ must not hash equally; and a live projection holds what a replay of the log holds.
findings.mechanism: JSON cannot tell those values apart, and the in-memory record never made the round trip the log's readers make.
findings.reproduction: scratchpad repro/round_trip.py: append payload {'deps': ('x', 'y'), 'm': {1: 'one'}}; compare with the replayed event.
findings.observed: hash equal: True; payload equal: False; written {'deps': ('x', 'y'), 'm': {1: 'one'}}, replayed {'deps': ['x', 'y'], 'm': {'1': 'one'}}.
findings.expected: The writer is handed the record as its canonical bytes parse back.
findings.correction: _write_event normalizes the body through json.loads(canonical_bytes(body)) before building the Event; the bytes written are unchanged. canonical.py's docstring states which Python values serialize alike.
findings.residual_risk: No production writer was found relying on a tuple or non-string key surviving its own append; the class is closed at the write rather than audited caller by caller.

findings.title: check_against calls an intact log truncated when a checkpoint is taken in the crash window that leaves the witness one record behind
findings.behavior: The witness is written after the append it describes, so a crash between the two leaves it one record behind the log; verify() reports that as a note and the log as ok. checkpoint.create() then checkpoints the log's head, one past the witness. check_against refused every checkpoint ahead of the witness as 'the log was truncated after the checkpoint'. verify_with, read_verified_with (AuthorityStore.load_from) and describes (prune and restore decisions) all call it.
findings.invariant: A checkpoint is refused for what is wrong with it; the module's two readers of the witness (verify and check_against) say the same thing about the same log.
findings.mechanism: The witness comparison could not tell the crash signature from a rolled-back witness, and named both truncation.
findings.observed: verify: ok=True with the note 'witness is behind the log (2 < 3)'; checkpoint created at seq 3; check_against: CheckpointAheadOfLog 'checkpoint names seq 3 but the head witness records 2; the log was truncated after the checkpoint'. The log was intact.
findings.expected: A witness one behind the checkpoint, with the checkpoint's record still at its offset, is the crash signature and stands; further behind is a rolled-back witness and is refused, as test C5 (test_a_rolled_back_head_witness_invalidates_a_checkpoint) already requires.
findings.correction: check_against accepts exactly the crash signature -- witness.seq == cp.seq - 1 and EventLog.check_anchor finds the checkpoint's record -- and refuses everything else as before, with a message that names a rolled-back witness as well as truncation.
findings.residual_risk: A witness rolled back by exactly one record is indistinguishable from the crash signature, here as in verify(). The cost of the defect was recovery time and a false diagnosis, not authority: load_from fell back to an older checkpoint or a full replay.

findings.title: Governed operations re-read the whole history: the records parsed by full verified reads grow quadratically with the campaign
findings.behavior: Counted by tools/work_counts.py under the scripted research-horizon campaign (SCRIPTED DECISIONS, no model): at 15, 30 and 60 decisions the full verified reads number 78, 114 and 198 and parse 11,195, 23,720 and 67,591 records. Doubling the campaign multiplied the records by 2.12 and then 2.85, approaching the x4 of quadratic work. At 60 decisions GovernedTasks.projection() (_verified_events) made 80 of the 198 full reads and parsed 28,337 records, 42% of the total; governed_model._view 20 reads; research.load 17; policy.load 12; and each GovernedTasks construction loads seven stores, each with its own full read.
findings.invariant: Directive Phase 2C: distinguish O(history) initialization, O(new) incremental operations and O(history^2) cumulative workloads caused by repeated full replay; count work, not wall time.
findings.mechanism: Each governed run rebuilds the task projection from genesis several times, and each new runner re-loads every store from genesis; the anchored O(new) paths exist but these callers do not use them.
findings.reproduction: python tools/work_counts.py --sizes 15,30,60 (docs/audit/work_counts.json); the same instrument at b0058f6 for the baseline.
findings.observed: At the baseline b0058f6 the same campaign also made 33, 48 and 89 anchor_at calls, each a second read of the log, parsing 3,552, 8,211 and 27,777 lines (x2.31, then x3.38: quadratic as well). The AUD-003 repair removed every one: at 60 decisions the lines parsed fell from 95,368 to 67,591 (-29%). Wall time is subprocess-dominated and did not move outside noise (20.5 s and 21.6 s at 60 decisions, measured back to back), which is the trap the directive names: the time hides the work.
findings.expected: Per governed operation, O(new) verification work after one O(history) load, with an explicit full-genesis path kept for readers that must start from nothing.
findings.correction: Partly made: AUD-003 (anchors from the verified read) removed the anchor_at re-reads. Not made, by an earlier decision: the governed projection re-verifies the whole chain on every fold, which docs/tranche_h/FINAL_REPORT.md ('Why the cost grows') states as deliberate -- an anchored read 're-reads no prefix and trusts the anchor', and moving the governed projection onto it 'would weaken a control to buy throughput'. The audit's reading of that trade: advance() is a verified read of the suffix, and require_extends (AUD-006) refuses a re-chained prefix in O(1), because the record at the projection's position must still carry the hash folded there. What an anchored fold gives up is in-process detection of later, unchained damage to the prefix already verified, which the next full read still finds: detection latency, not the correctness of decisions made against the verified state. The options are the owner's: keep the full re-verification and accept the measured growth; fold anchored with require_extends and re-verify from genesis every K folds or T seconds, which bounds the latency; or memoize the verified prefix by a digest of its bytes (the report's own proposal), which still reads and hashes the prefix on every fold but no longer parses it.
findings.residual_risk: Measured: at 60 scripted decisions, 198 full reads parse 67,591 records (docs/audit/work_counts.json). In the recorded Gate G campaign (docs/assurance/research_horizon_results.json, 8f53500) a decision took 0.56 s at the 50 stage and 2.33 s at the 1,000 stage, and the 5,000 and 10,000 stages were not reached (FINAL_REPORT.md projects about 10 and 31 more hours).

findings.title: Authority-record roles are self-asserted: nothing binds the actor of a VERIFIED or PROMOTED transition to the role it claims

files.lines: check(): the role must be one the edge permits
RegisteredKey: a key binds a principal, not a role
_check_may_register(): only a HUMAN principal's registrar is checked
RoleRegistry, RoleView, RoleDelegations: the root, the question and the delegations

findings.behavior: check() requires the role a transition claims to be one its edge permits, and requires the actor to differ from the proposer where the edge says so (I4). The role itself is taken from the request (live) or the record's payload (replay). Neither reader consults the agent directory, the key registry (whose entries bind a key to a principal and carry no role) or the policy the promotion cites (_policy_refusal checks its publisher, withdrawal and expiry, not who may promote under it). So one identity may verify and promote, and an identity registered nowhere may take every role but the proposer's.
findings.invariant: AGENT_SUBSTRATE.md: a PROMOTED record 'means a claim was proposed, independently verified, and promoted under a recorded policy'; authority.py: Role is 'who may act'.
findings.mechanism: Roles are compared with the edge, never with an authority that grants them. The governed task layer checks the agent directory (GovernedTasks requires the verifier to hold AgentRole.VERIFIER there), and the directory admits an AGENT with any roles from any registrar, registered or not: _check_may_register guards HUMAN principals only. So the governed layer's role is a registration anyone can make, and the authority store beneath it asks for none.
findings.observed: 'mallory', registered nowhere, moved alice's claim UNDER_REVIEW (VERIFIER), VERIFIED (VERIFIER) and PROMOTED (PROMOTER, policy p1): the store holds it PROMOTED and canonical, and the second reader agrees with nothing unauthorized. And 'mallory', registered nowhere, registered an AGENT v-evil holding VERIFIER (and 'nobody-at-all' one holding EXECUTOR): require() passes for both and a replay keeps them; a HUMAN registered by mallory is refused.
findings.expected: Before any production path reaches PROMOTED: an authority outside the log -- as the key registry is -- or the cited promotion policy names who may verify and who may promote, and both readers refuse anyone else.
findings.correction: agent_substrate/roles.py: a role registry supplied from outside the log and pinned by its digest, as the key registry is. Each grant names a principal, a role, a scope and the positions it holds for. Delegation happens once, in the log, from grants marked may_delegate (PROPOSER, EXECUTOR, VERIFIER, PROMOTER only); it is never made to the delegator, never wider or longer than its parent, and revoked by its delegator. A reader given a registry holds each act to it before the record is written and again on every replay. AuthorityStore: create needs PROPOSER over kind:<kind>; a transition needs the role it claims, and SYSTEM needs VERIFIER or PROMOTER. PolicyStore and the AuthorityStore's own policy fold: POLICY_OWNER. GovernedTasks: PROPOSER, EXECUTOR and VERIFIER over tool:<tool id>, each where its record is written. The rules are restated in reconstruct, reconstruct_tasks and reconstruct_subsystems. Under a registry, agent registration confers nothing, and a checkpoint folded under other grants is not restored. Which principals hold which roles in production, and provisioning the registry, remain the owner's: production_role_registry refuses until then.
findings.residual_risk: Enforced only by a reader given a registry, as authentication is only by a reader given an authenticator. No history declaration yet obliges a reader to hold a registry; a genesis declaration like AUTHENTICATED_REQUIRED would. No production registry is provisioned, which is an owner action. HUMAN_APPROVER and RELEASE_AUTHORITY can be granted and are consumed by nothing yet: an escalation's answer still rests on the directory's HUMAN principal. SCHEDULER and SYSTEM task moves are held to the edge alone. Without AUTHENTICATED_REQUIRED a name is unauthenticated, and a writer able to append can write under a holder's name. Collusion among grantees remains the documented separation-of-duties limit. Mutations RA1-RA36 and RR1-RR8 (tools/mutations/role_authority.json) are each killed.

findings.title: An AUTHENTICATED_REQUIRED history reads as authenticated to an authenticator that asks only some actors

files.lines: _security_gate(): the authenticator's report is taken as the verdict
authenticate(): an actor outside require is not asked; Authenticator.require; production_authenticator(require=)
reconstruct(): the second reader's own authentication verdict

findings.behavior: Under AUTHENTICATED_REQUIRED the read primitives refused a reader given no authenticator and otherwise took the authenticator's report. principals.authenticate(require=...) checks only the actors it names and passes every other event without asking, and both Authenticator and production_authenticator accept require. So a REQUIRED history read through an authenticator scoped to some actors -- or to none, require=frozenset() -- read a correctly chained, unsigned record by any other name as authenticated, whether or not the deployment pinned the profile. A writer holding that authenticator appended after the record, and the second reader, whose own verdict is the same authenticator's, folded it.
findings.invariant: events.py, the security profile: 'AUTHENTICATED_REQUIRED means every event must be authenticated, and it is enforced HERE, in the verified-read primitives every reader in this package reads through, so a reader cannot skip authentication by leaving out one optional argument'.
findings.mechanism: The gate checked that an authenticator was present, not that it asked every actor. The scope that makes require useful on a legacy history was honoured on a REQUIRED one.
findings.observed: A REQUIRED history (the declaration by owner, one record by alice) and a correctly chained, unsigned record by mallory, an actor with no key, written into the file. require=None: ok=False, NO_KEY for mallory, and the read stops before the record. require={'alice'}: ok=True and the record read, with required_profile pinned to AUTHENTICATED_REQUIRED or not. A signed append by alice through the scoped log wrote seq 3 after it, and reconstruct() with the scoped authenticator folded r1, r2 (mallory's) and r3 with nothing unauthorized. The same at the audit baseline b0058f6.
findings.expected: A REQUIRED history is read only through an authenticator that asks every actor; one that names a scope reads nothing of it, and the second reader refuses it in its own code as it refuses a missing authenticator.
findings.correction: _security_gate refuses a REQUIRED, non-empty history to an authenticator whose require is not None, with a problem naming the scope, before asking it anything; the anchored read and the writer's head check go through the same gate. reconstruct() restates the rule: given a scoped authenticator for a history whose genesis declares REQUIRED, it folds nothing and says why. On a legacy history require keeps its meaning.
regression_tests: tests/test_authenticated_history.py::test_a_required_history_is_not_read_by_an_authenticator_asking_some (6 cases: three scopes, the profile pinned and not)
findings.residual_risk: The gate trusts the authenticator object it is handed: it reads the scope an Authenticator declares, and a callable that skips actors without declaring a scope is not detected. No reader in the repository was configured with a scope, and production authentication is not provisioned (no registry, no vetted provider), so nothing deployed was exposed. Roles remain self-asserted under authentication (AUD-011).

findings.title: The long-horizon campaign cannot resume after its process dies: a stopped campaign starts again from nothing

files.lines: Campaign.__init__, _save, _resume, run(), invalidate_one(), measure(), main(): the state beside the world, the lock, the resume
World.__init__: resume=True opens an existing workspace and writes no bootstrap

findings.behavior: World(name) deletes any workspace of that name before it builds a fresh one, and main() deletes the workspace when the run ends, normally or not. The campaign's own counters (resets, restarts, recovery failures, objectives, the stage clock) live in its process. Inside it, the governed loop does recover a crash mid-step from the log, in a freshly built controller, but only within the same process. Nothing resumes the campaign itself.
findings.invariant: The audit directive, phase 9: a long-horizon campaign that resumes across the death of its process. FINAL_REPORT.md names the same change: 'A resumable campaign that persists its counters beside the world and finishes the objective in flight. That is also a whole-process recovery test.'
findings.mechanism: State the campaign keeps outside the log lives only in its process, and its workspace is deleted on construction and on exit.
findings.reproduction: Read: tools/adversarial_eval.py World.__init__ (shutil.rmtree of an existing base) and clean(); tools/research_horizon.py main(). Recorded: docs/assurance/research_horizon_results.json at 8f53500.
findings.observed: The recorded run asked for 10,000 decisions and holds the 50, 100 and 1,000 stages with complete=false. FINAL_REPORT.md says the process went with a reclaimed container after 1,547 decisions in 76 minutes, and the 5,000 and 10,000 stages are not claimed.
findings.expected: Counters and stage bookkeeping that persist beside the world, and a campaign resumed from the log in a new process that reaches the counters an uninterrupted run reaches.
findings.correction: tools/research_horizon.py keeps the campaign's own state in campaign_state.json beside the world. The file is written atomically (a temporary file, fsync, os.replace and a directory fsync) before each objective, after each stage and after each withdrawal, and it is bound to the log position (seq, hash) it describes. --resume opens the same world without rebuilding it (World(resume=True)). The log is the authority over what happened. A log that no longer holds the recorded position, because it was rolled back or rewritten, is refused. The log may register one objective more than the state records. If that objective is still OPEN, a new controller finishes it. If it was finished before the process died, it is counted once. A stage measured and not saved is measured again, and a withdrawal the dead process made and did not record is settled (GovernedModelRuns.settle) and not repeated. One process holds a campaign at a time, through an flock the kernel releases when the process dies. The workspace is kept when a run stops. Counters derived from the log cannot be counted twice. process_restarts counts the campaign's own resumptions, and restarts still counts scripted crashes in a process that lived to record them.
findings.residual_risk: The state survives only where the workspace survives. A machine reclaimed with its disk takes both, as the recorded 10,000-decision run's container did, and resuming that needs durable storage a deployment provides. A process killed between the two halves of a stage boundary's withdrawal (the task, then its bytes) is settled, but the second half is not made again; no test reaches that point. The scripted fault of the objective in flight is lost with the process, so restarts can read one lower than in an uninterrupted run, while every counter taken from the log agrees. The 5,000 and 10,000 stages have still not been run. Twelve kill points are tested, each in a separate process killed with os._exit, with every action-level difference from an uninterrupted run named: a stage's checkpoint measured again, and one context assembled for a model call that was never made. Mutations RHR1-RHR11 (tools/mutations/research_horizon_resume.json).

findings.title: A refused mint is written before it is refused: one call leaves a capability log that no reader will load again

files.lines: CapabilityLedger.issue(): decide() appended the grant without asking who may mint; _authorize_mint() ran only in apply()
DecidedWriter._append_decided(): the record is written, then folded

findings.behavior: issue() decided the record under the writer lock and checked its id, its start and its terms, but not who may mint it. The rule -- the root mints, a holder delegates an attenuation -- lived in _authorize_mint(), which apply() runs on the record after DecidedWriter._append_decided() has written it. So a mint by any actor other than the root was durable before it was refused: the caller got NotTheIssuer, the log kept the record, and every later CapabilityLedger.load() of that log refused the whole history at its seq. The same for a delegation by an actor that does not hold the parent, written through issue() rather than delegate().
findings.invariant: events.py, DecidedWriter: a decision is taken under the writer lock so that a refused write is 'refused before anything is written instead of leaving a history every later load refuses'; capability.py, issue(), of its other checks: 'Refused here, under the lock, nothing is written.' The live path and every replay apply one rule to one record.
findings.mechanism: The live path and the fold asked different questions, and the fold's answer arrived after the append.
findings.observed: A ledger whose root is 'scheduler' with one grant: issue(..., actor='mallory') raised NotTheIssuer, the log went from 2 records to 3 (the last by mallory), and a fresh load raised NotTheIssuer at seq 2 -- while the live ledger kept answering as if nothing had happened. The same at the baseline b0058f6.
findings.expected: The mint refused before anything is written: the log unchanged, and a fresh load as before.
findings.correction: issue()'s decide() runs _authorize_mint() on the record it is about to write (its seq and actor), under the writer lock and after the fold of what other writers appended, so the live path and replay apply one rule and a refusal writes nothing. delegate() and revoke() already decided their rules before writing.
regression_tests: tests/test_agent_delegation.py::test_a_refused_mint_never_reaches_the_log (with the root's mint and a holder's delegation as the control)
findings.residual_risk: The same shape -- a fold that refuses a record its own writer wrote -- was looked for here, in the capability ledger. It was not looked for systematically in every DecidedWriter; a property that every refused write leaves the log unchanged, across writers, does not exist yet. Under AUTHENTICATED_REQUIRED an unsigned write is refused before it is written, so the exposure is to legacy histories, which is every history in this repository.

findings.title: Anyone may publish the next version of an owner's policy, and a policy-bound promotion then stands on it

files.lines: PolicyStore.publish() and apply(): a later version was checked for order and withdrawal, not for who published it
_fold_policy_record(): the binding's view kept the first version's publisher, and took expiry from the latest version

findings.behavior: A policy's owner is whoever published version 1, and only the owner may withdraw it. Publishing the next version was anyone's: publish() and its replay checked that the version followed the last and that the policy was not withdrawn. The new version then governed every PolicyStore decision after it. Where a history binds its promotions to named policy authorities, the store and the second reader both judged a promotion by the publisher of the policy's FIRST version, while its expiry came from the latest. So an outsider's version 2 replaced the owner's rules and lifted the owner's expiry, and promotions under the policy were admitted on it.
findings.invariant: tests/test_policy_binding.py (D-2026-148): 'a policy's owner (whoever published version 1) may WITHDRAW it'; 'a promotion's policy must be published on that history by one of them [the named principals], not withdrawn, and not expired at the promotion'.
findings.mechanism: Ownership governed withdrawal only, and the binding asked who published the policy's first version rather than the version in force.
findings.observed: On a history bound to 'policy-authority': 'mallory' published version 2 of the authority's policy p1 without its expiry, and it was accepted live and on replay. After version 1 expired, a promotion under p1 was PROMOTED, standing on mallory's version. The same at the baseline b0058f6.
findings.expected: A later version by anyone but the owner refused, live before it is written and on replay. A binding judges the publisher of the version in force, so a promotion standing on an outsider's version is refused by both readers.
findings.correction: PolicyStore.publish() refuses a later version by anyone but the owner, under the writer lock after the version checks, so nothing is written; apply() refuses the same record on replay. The store's binding view and the second reader's take the publisher of the latest version, so a promotion under a policy whose version in force an outsider wrote is refused, live and on replay. The second reader's subsystem replay notes the version and does not fold it.
regression_tests: tests/test_policy_binding.py::test_only_the_owner_publishes_a_later_version (with the owner's version 2 as the control)
findings.residual_risk: Ownership is still first-come: whoever publishes version 1 of an id owns it, and nothing names who may create a policy. That is the open publishing the binding was built around. Owners and policy authorities are names: authenticated under AUTHENTICATED_REQUIRED, self-asserted otherwise (AUD-011).

findings.title: The process-tree negative control leaves the grandchild it shows escaping running after the test

files.lines: _TREE, ESCAPEE_SECONDS and probe_process_tree(): the grandchild looped forever and nothing stopped it

findings.behavior: With isolation switched off on purpose, the probe's grandchild -- in a session of its own -- outlives the tool killed on timeout, which is what the negative control asserts. Nothing then stops it: it is reparented to the host's init and writes out/beat every 100 ms until its directory is deleted (pytest prunes a run's temporary directory after three newer runs; a CI runner is discarded).
findings.invariant: A test leaves no process behind it.
findings.mechanism: The probe measures the escape and returns; the escaped process has no stop condition.
findings.reproduction: During the full suite at d3cddc3: a python process running the _TREE loop, parent PID 1, cwd /tmp/pytest-of-root/pytest-179/test_each_probe_sees_the_bound3, still writing after the test had passed.
findings.observed: One orphan per run of the suite, alive until its temporary directory is pruned.
findings.expected: The grandchild stops once the probe has measured it.
findings.correction: The grandchild beats while out/stop does not exist and until its own bound (ESCAPEE_SECONDS, 30 s) passes. The probe takes both readings, then writes out/stop in a finally, so a probe that raises still writes it. The bound ends the grandchild of a probe stopped before the finally runs, such as by a kill or a test timeout. Neither runs before the reading, and the verdict is unchanged. No PID is used: under a PID namespace the recorded PID is the namespace's and names an unrelated process on the host.
findings.residual_risk: A probe killed before its finally leaves the grandchild running for at most ESCAPEE_SECONDS. The tests find a leftover by its working directory, through /proc. That needs Linux and permission to read another process's cwd. Each test also kills what it finds, so a mutant that leaves the grandchild running does not outlive its test. Both tests failed before the fix, each leaving one process, which the test killed. Mutations IS11 (no stop file), IS12 (no bound) and IS13 (a bound shorter than the reading) are each killed, and IS7 still is.

findings.title: Nothing says who may issue a secret grant or an egress grant

files.lines: SecretStore.issue() and apply(): a grant's id, digest and stamp are checked on both paths, and its issuer on neither
NetworkAuthority.issue(): an egress grant's id and stamp are checked, and its issuer is not
SECRET_ISSUER and EGRESS_ISSUER, granted by the registry

findings.behavior: SecretStore.issue() and its replay check that a grant's id is new, that its digest matches and that its start is the log's stamp; revocation is the granter's alone, on both paths. Who may ISSUE a grant is checked on neither, so any actor that can append may grant itself access to any registered secret. The capability ledger closed the same gap with a root issuer (tests/test_agent_delegation.py states it as found: 'no ISSUER authority: any actor that can write the log can mint a grant'); the secret store has none. NetworkAuthority.issue() is the same: an egress grant's id and stamp are checked, its issuer is not. Egress grants ARE decided on the governed path: socket_guard(self.network, actor=..., task_id=...) wraps a task's execution and verification in GovernedTasks, mediating the runner process's own sockets (a tool's child has no network either way, by its namespace).
findings.invariant: secrets.py: a value is 'reachable only through SecretStore.resolve, only under a grant that names the actor, task, tool and purpose' -- which binds the grant's use, not its making.
findings.mechanism: Issuance authority was given to capability grants and not to secret grants.
findings.reproduction: Read: SecretStore.issue() and apply() (agent_substrate/secrets.py); NetworkAuthority.issue() (agent_substrate/netauth.py). Reachability: no module in agent_substrate/ or tools/ calls SecretStore.resolve(); GovernedTasks calls socket_guard over the network authority at three sites.
findings.observed: By reading, not executed. Secret grants: no governed path resolves one in this build. Egress grants: an actor that can append can grant the runner's mediated egress for a task, which the socket guard then permits; mediation of the runner's own sockets, not of the tool's child.
findings.expected: An issuer authority for secret and egress grants, as the capability ledger has, held on both paths -- for egress before any deployment relies on the mediation, for secrets before a governed path first resolves one.
findings.correction: Under a role registry (agent_substrate/roles.py), a secret grant is issued only by a principal the registry grants SECRET_ISSUER over secret:<secret id>. An egress grant is issued only by one granted EGRESS_ISSUER over egress:<host>, for every host the grant names. Both are decided under the writer lock before the record exists, refused again on replay by SecretStore and NetworkAuthority, and restated by reconstruct_subsystems. Neither issuing role may be delegated. Revocation stays the granter's. Who issues in production is the owner's to provision.
findings.residual_risk: Enforced only where the store is given a registry. No production registry is provisioned. Egress mediation remains an application control over the runner's own sockets, and the kernel network namespace still contains a tool. Mutations RA25-RA29 and RR6 are each killed.
